o: Free AI tools that actually work, no coding needed: KAFA ASİSTAN, MAHKEME and more.
Vibe Kafası Academy | Build Software with AI from Zero
Learn to build software with AI from zero, no coding needed: short, practical, free lessons with examples, plus a glossary of terms.
Vibe Kafası Academy graduation: finish 52 lessons, collect the badges, pass the exam and get a shareable graduate card and certificate.
Vibe Kafası Academy graduates: people who learned to build software with AI from zero and passed the final exam.
Vibe Coding Glossary: AI and Software Terms
156 software and AI terms in plain English for beginners: API, token, terminal, deploy, Git and more.
Vibe Kafası videos: funny yet educational shorts with Serdar, Claude and Codex (in Turkish), each linked to its lesson.
KAFA ASİSTAN sample panel: your day, tasks, notes and goals on one screen. Control it with hand gestures via camera and with your voice.
KAFA ASİSTAN user guide: 5-step setup, every command, the panel, hand gestures, facial expressions and troubleshooting.
A chat assistant answers; an agent does the work. Learn how an AI agent works, what it can do and how to manage it safely.
What is a domain name, how does DNS work, and what are A and CNAME records for? Steps to connect your own domain to your site, plus security notes.
What is an API? What is an API key for?
An API is the door programs use to request services from each other. Learn APIs, API keys and the rules for keeping keys safe with a waiter analogy.
Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor: which one is for what?
Learn the difference between a chat assistant, a coding agent and an AI code editor, and use Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex and Cursor in the right place.
Context window, tokens and usage limits
What are tokens, the context window and usage limits? Why does AI “forget,” why do limits run out, and how do you keep your chats tidy?
Experiment on a branch without breaking the main project, then review and merge changes with a pull request. Step-by-step commands and GitHub screens.
A 10-minute checklist to run before your site goes live: phone view, links, secret keys, speed, HTTPS and a rollback plan.
Installing Claude Code and your first task
Install Claude Code on macOS, Linux and Windows with the official commands, sign in and give it its first task. Requirements and basic commands.
Install Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, with the official commands, sign in with your ChatGPT account, set permissions and give it its first task.
Rules for running several AI agents on one project without them stepping on each other: separate tasks, separate folders, separate ports, one coordinator.
What is deploying? Local vs. live
Deploying means taking your project off your computer and putting it at an address anyone can open. Learn the differences and traps between local and live.
Find a problem people pay to solve
A good product idea comes from a problem people already spend time or money to solve. Learn how to find such problems and how to test them.
See what the AI changed with git diff. Undo safely with restore and revert, and learn why reset --hard and force push are dangerous.
What do file, folder, extension and path mean? Learn the concepts you'll meet most when building projects with AI, using an address analogy.
Code editors: VS Code and friends
What is a code editor, and why start with VS Code? Installing it, opening a folder, the built-in terminal and picking safe extensions, step by step.
What are the frontend, the backend and the database? Learn the three layers of an app with a restaurant analogy, and which projects need which.
Git is a free program that keeps save points for your project. Learn how Git differs from GitHub, the key terms and the first-time setup.
Publish a static site for free: GitHub Pages
Publish your HTML, CSS and JavaScript site for free with GitHub Pages. Setup steps, how the address works and common mistakes.
GitHub: put your code in the cloud
Create a repository on GitHub, send your project to the cloud with push, get it back with pull and clone. Learn public vs. private repos.
Keep your API key safe: .env and .gitignore
Keep API keys in a .env file and stop them reaching GitHub with .gitignore. Learn what to do first if a key leaks.
When does AI make things up, and how do you catch it?
AI sometimes states things that aren't true with full confidence. Learn where hallucinations show up most and practical ways to catch them.
Debugging: console, logs, step by step
Learn to open the browser console, read error messages, trace your code with console.log and narrow a bug down step by step.
Don't just say "it doesn't work": paste the error message
When something breaks, give AI what you did, what you expected, what happened and the full error message, so it can fix the problem on the first try.
Your first commit: add, commit, log
Create your first save point with git init, status, add, commit and log. Learn what the staging area is and how to write a good commit message.
Day one: sign up and build your first mini app without installing anything
Without installing anything, using only your browser, build your first mini app in Claude or ChatGPT: a profit calculator, step by step.
Step by step: a one-page website
Build your first one-page website with AI: create a folder, make an index.html file, see it in your browser and improve it in small steps.
How do you write a good prompt?
Learn how to write a request that gets you the result you want from AI: context, goal, details, limits and output format, plus a ready-made template.
What are JSON and CSV, and when do you use each? Learn their rules, common mistakes and the garbled-character problem, with examples.
What are code and programming languages? (HTML, JavaScript, Python)
What is code, and what is a programming language for? Meet HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python through a house analogy and run your first code in the browser.
Learn to give AI work in small pieces and set limits like “only touch this file,” then check the result after every step.
User data and passwords: the basic rules
Collect as little user data as you can, never store passwords as plain text, use ready-made login systems. For laws like GDPR, ask an expert.
Stop repeating yourself every session: write CLAUDE.md for Claude Code and AGENTS.md for Codex. Where they go, /init, and a sample rules file.
Where do the costs of an AI-built product come from? Get to know subscriptions, APIs, servers and other costs; tell revenue from profit; set spending limits.
MCP is the common standard that connects AI to outside services like calendars, files and databases. Learn to add a connector in Claude and use it safely.
MVP: the smallest product that works
An MVP is the smallest working product that tests your most important assumption with real users. Learn what to cut, what to do by hand and what to measure.
What can you build with vibe coding, and what is hard?
Learn to sort ideas with a traffic-light method: what vibe coding handles easily, what needs care, and what needs an expert.
Node.js, Python and package managers (npm, pip)
What are Node.js and Python, and how do you install them? Learn to install packages with npm and pip, virtual environments and safe package choices.
Instead of having AI write code right away, learn to make a plan first: ask questions, read the plan, approve it, build step by step and check.
Sell first: pre-sales and your first customer
Before you build, see whether someone will really pay. A practical guide to pre-sales, finding your first customer and telling revenue from profit.
Turn the jobs you repeat every day into flows that run on their own. Learn how triggers work, what n8n is and how scheduled tasks run.
Pick a small project and narrow the scope
For your first project, skip the big dream and pick a small job you can finish in a week. Learn how to narrow your idea and define “done.”
What is a skill, and how do you install one?
A skill is an instruction package that teaches Claude to do a job equally well every time. Learn what it is, how to install it and the safety rules.
You finished the course, so what now? A 30-day practice plan to make it stick, free official resources and the rules to carry into every project.
What is the terminal? Your first 6 commands, no fear
Open the terminal and learn your first 6 commands: where you are, listing, entering folders, creating folders and files, on macOS, Linux and Windows.
The job isn't done just because AI says “done.” Learn a manual testing checklist and automated tests that check code with code, with simple examples.
Publish your site automatically from GitHub with Vercel and Netlify, get a preview link for every change, and roll back if something breaks.
Vibe coding means describing what you want in plain words and letting AI write the code. Learn how it works, what changed and what didn't.
How does a website work? (browser, server, domain)
What happens behind the scenes when you type a site into the address bar? Learn browsers, servers, domains, DNS and HTTPS step by step with a mail analogy.
How does AI work? (language model, tokens, prediction)
What is the language model behind Claude and ChatGPT, what are tokens, and why does AI sometimes make things up? Explained with a phone keyboard analogy.
Back up, then test the restore
Learn what to back up, where and how often. Apply the 3-2-1 rule, and don't trust a backup you've never tried to restore.
Run the project on your own computer (localhost, port)
What are localhost and ports? Run your project on your own computer with a small server, and easily fix the most common errors.
Set permission and spending limits for agents
Use permission settings in Claude Code and Codex, and spending limits in API dashboards. Give an agent only the access its job needs.
What do I type every day?
A backup rule: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 kept off-site.
The fee you pay regularly to use a tool, and the usage you get in return.
Software whose source code is public and can be used and changed according to its license.
A rules file in a shared format read by Codex and many other coding agents.
AI that takes a goal and does the work itself using tools: reads and changes files, runs commands, checks the result.
An easy-to-remember internet address like myshop.com.
A helper agent the main agent hands a job to; it works in its own context window and returns only a summary.
An address made by adding a word in front of the main domain: www.myshop.com, blog.myshop.com and so on.
The branch where the real, working version of the project lives; usually named main.
A long secret password that identifies you when using an API; usage and charges go to the key's owner.
A door with clear rules through which two programs ask each other for information or services.
The part that runs on the server, unseen by the user, doing the real work: login checks, saving orders, payments.
Claude showing larger outputs, like a small web app, working in a separate panel next to the chat.
Other packages a project needs to run; their list is kept in a file.
How much text the model can keep in front of it at once while answering; its working memory.
A ready-made connection, usually built on MCP, that links Claude to a service in a few clicks.
A service that keeps a site's or app's files on a server reachable from the internet at all times.
The program (shell) that interprets the commands you type in the terminal, used on Linux and many servers.
The date the model's training text ends; it can only learn about later events through a tool like web search.
A parallel line of work opened without disturbing the main line.
What happens during a merge when two branches changed the same line of the same file differently.
The version of the project that is online and used by real users.
A large code foundation that provides an app's skeleton, rules and ready-made parts.
OpenAI's AI assistant; it runs in the browser and in the desktop and mobile apps.
The total money coming in from sales, before expenses are taken out.
Anthropic's coding agent: it reads and edits files in your project folder, runs commands and tests.
Anthropic's web dashboard for developers, where API keys, usage, invoices and spending limits are managed.
The rules file Claude Code reads at the start of every session.
Anthropic's AI assistant; it runs in the browser and in the desktop and mobile apps.
Copying an entire remote repository, with its whole history, onto your own computer.
OpenAI's coding agent: it reads and writes code, runs commands and presents changes for you to review.
A record of the project's current state with a short note attached.
A short time formula that says when a job should run, using five fields.
The language that sets how a web page looks: colors, fonts, spacing and layout on phones.
A plain-text version of a table: each row is a record and values are separated by commas.
A VS Code–based code editor with an AI agent built in.
Telling the AI clearly which files it may and may not touch in a task.
A cost that grows as sales or usage grow.
A box in which a program stores a piece of information under a name and can change it when needed.
Taking a project from your computer and putting it on a server anyone can open; in other words, publishing it.
A line-by-line list of the differences between two states: what was added and what was removed.
A program trained on a huge amount of text that writes by predicting the most likely next piece of a text.
A site that builds the page for each visitor on the spot, with a program, and usually a database, running behind it.
A one-line setting that tells a domain name where to go.
The system that turns a domain name into the IP address computers understand; the internet's phone book.
The official documents that explain how to use a tool, language or API.
A single named piece of information on a computer: a photo, a document or the code of a web page.
A short command for the tool itself that you type into the agent's chat box starting with /.
A small piece added to a program later that gives it new features.
What is Principle of least privilege?
Giving a person or agent only as much permission as they need to do their job.
A file in the project folder where secret settings like API keys are kept in NAME=value form.
A named piece of code that does a specific job and can be called again and again.
The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which governs the protection of personal data.
Canceling a change or commit in Git and returning the project to its earlier state.
Bringing files or a database back from a backup and returning to the earlier working state.
A program that saves a project's history step by step, shows what changed and lets you go back to an earlier state.
A free service that publishes the HTML, CSS and JavaScript files in a GitHub repo at a web address.
A service that stores projects saved with Git online and makes sharing and collaboration possible.
A list that tells Git which files and folders it should never track.
When AI states something that isn't true with great confidence, as if it were a fact.
A setting on an API account that caps how much money can be spent in a given period.
A one-way process that turns text into a fixed-length code that can't be reversed; passwords are stored this way.
The work of finding where a bug is in software and fixing it.
Text that explains what broke, and where, when a program goes wrong.
The in-between area where you choose and place the changes that will go into the next commit.
A cap on how many requests or tokens can be sent to an API within a given time.
The markup language that defines what is on a web page: the heading, paragraph, image and button.
The shared language the browser and server use to send requests and get responses.
The encrypted version of HTTP: it makes the data between browser and server unreadable on the way.
Asking for a second proof at login besides your password, such as a code on your phone.
A website's home page file; the first page sent to the browser when a folder is opened.
The numeric address of every device connected to the internet.
An automation chain that starts with a trigger and runs through steps in order.
The message or instruction in which you tell the AI what you want.
An attempt to steer AI into unwanted actions with instructions hidden in a web page, file or tool.
The setting that decides which actions an agent may take without asking you.
The programming language that gives a web page behavior: calculating when you click, opening a menu, fetching data.
A text format that stores information as label–value pairs; the format programs use most to send each other data.
The boundary of what a project or task includes and what it doesn't.
The money left in your hands after all expenses are taken out of revenue.
Checking that a user really is who they claim to be; usually signing in with a password.
Any information that identifies a person directly or indirectly, like name, phone, email or address.
A container that holds files and other folders together.
The program where you open, read, edit and run code files.
Instructions written in a programming language that tell the computer what to do, step by step.
A short instruction you type into the terminal and run with Enter.
The part of the browser's developer tools where the page's errors and log messages are shown.
The amount of AI use your plan allows within a certain time.
A file a coding agent reads at the start of each session, with working rules for the project and for you.
Turkey's Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698, which governs how personal data is processed in Turkey.
The address your computer gives itself; it lets you open a project running on a local server in the browser.
Lines a program leaves while running, saying “I'm here right now, and this is what I have.”
A stable program version that gets security and bug fixes for a long time.
A simple way to write formatted notes in plain text, using # for headings and - for bullet points.
A shared standard AI tools use to connect to outside services like calendars, file storage and GitHub.
Adding the changes from one branch to another, usually to the main branch.
A page adjusting itself properly to phone, tablet and computer screens.
The trained language model, with a name and version, that runs behind an AI tool.
The smallest working version of a product that solves the customer's core problem and tests your key assumption.
A visual tool where you build automation flows by connecting boxes.
A hosting platform similar to Vercel, offering automatic publishing from GitHub, preview links and serverless functions.
An environment that runs JavaScript code outside the browser, on your own computer or a server.
Node.js' package manager: it downloads ready-made code packages written by others and installs them in your project.
Measuring real demand by trying to sell a product before it's fully built.
The part of an app that appears on the user's screen and runs in their browser.
A version of a change published at a separate link without affecting the live site.
A setting the program reads from the environment it runs in, not written into the code; used for secret keys.
Having a repetitive job do itself, without you, once it's been set up.
A small piece of code saying “if I give this input, I expect this result” that reruns in seconds with one command.
A single work period you start with an AI tool, lasting until you close or clear it.
A tool that finds, downloads, installs and updates packages.
A ready-made piece of code written by others that you can add to your project and use.
An app that keeps your passwords and secret keys in an encrypted vault and generates strong passwords.
Python's package manager: it downloads and installs Python packages.
A mode in which the agent reads files and writes a plan but changes nothing until you approve.
The numbered door through which each server running on the same computer serves.
Windows' modern command line; on Windows, opening a terminal usually gets you this.
A language with its own rules in which instructions for a computer are written.
The main folder that holds all the files of a project.
A workspace in Claude that keeps the documents, instructions and chats for a specific job together.
A review and approval request opened on GitHub to add a branch's changes to the main branch.
Bringing new changes from the remote repository onto your own computer.
Sending the new commits on your computer to a remote repository like GitHub.
An easy-to-read programming language widely used for data processing and automation.
An intro file that explains what a project is and how to install and run it.
The project folder Git tracks, together with its whole history.
A cost that stays the same each period regardless of how many sales you make.
A random value unique to each user, added to a password before it's hashed.
A project-specific install area that keeps a Python project's packages separate from other projects.
An isolated environment where an agent or program can only touch the area it's allowed to.
Turning information into a form that only someone with the right key can open.
A folder that packages the instructions for a job, which Claude opens and uses on its own when needed.
An AI app that answers your messages in writing; Claude and ChatGPT are the best-known examples.
The language used to ask a database questions and to add, change and delete records.
A site that sends everyone the same HTML, CSS and JavaScript files, with no program running behind it.
A small piece of backend code on a hosting platform that runs only when it's called.
A computer that is always online, stores a site's or app's files and answers incoming requests.
The program that requests web pages and shows them on screen: Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox and so on.
A window where you give the computer commands by typing instead of clicking with the mouse.
Trying out whether a feature that was written really works as expected.
The event that starts an automation flow: a set time, a new order or a submitted form.
The small pieces AI splits text into when reading and writing; limits and API costs are measured in them.
The full address of a page or file on the internet.
A copy of the project kept somewhere else, usually on GitHub.
The part after the dot at the end of a file name that tells you the file's type.
A hosting platform that connects to your GitHub repo and publishes your site automatically on every git push.
A system that stores information in an organized, permanent way and finds what you need fast.
Building software by describing what you want in plain words and letting AI write the code, while you keep the direction and control.
Microsoft's free code editor that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
A separate folder copy of the same Git repo on its own branch; agents working in parallel don't mix up each other's files.
A Microsoft feature that lets you run a Linux environment inside Windows.
Computers doing jobs that normally take human intelligence, like writing, talking and seeing.
A copy of files, code or a database kept somewhere else in case of damage or deletion.
The version of the project that runs only on your computer.
Deciding what an authenticated user is allowed to see and do.
The full address of a file or folder on your computer.
